title: I shipped a mobile roguelike on both stores after 3 months of directing Claude Code. How the work actually went, including what it got wrong.
author: Hot_Ad_9834
selftext:
Solo dev from Korea. I grew up on Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup and wanted a one-thumb version for my phone, so I made one with Claude Code and Godot. It's out on the App Store and Google Play now. This post is about how the work actually went, not a highlight reel.



The split: I didn't write code or draw a sprite. I decided what the game is, played every build on my phone, looked at every screenshot and clip it produced, and said what was wrong. Claude did the rest: the code, the sprites (generated by scripts), the sound (synthesized), the store listings, the Firebase leaderboard, the AdMob integration, the iOS and Android build pipelines. It even set up our Discord server through the API.



How a typical feature went:



1. I say what I want in a sentence or two, usually in Korean, usually blunt. "The early floors are boring." "The map looks flat." "This icon is bad."



2. For anything with taste in it (art, UI, store images) I make it produce several drafts side by side, A/B/C. I pick one, or say none of them. Describing what I wanted never worked. Picking did.



3. It writes the chosen approach into a design doc with the date and the reason, builds it, runs the tests, then screenshots the result for me.



4. I play it on the phone. Most of the time something is off that no test caught. Back to step 1.



How many rounds things really took, because this is the part people underestimate:



\- Sprites: the entire art set was rewritten three times. Round one was flat and faced the wrong way. Round two, a small tool that builds each character out of 3D blobs and renders it down to pixels, I liked. It then "improved" that into a round three I hated, so we went back to round two and it redrew all 380 sheets with it.



\- App icon: a dozen rounds of drafts. At one point I told it to go study the top roguelike icons on the store. It pulled them through the iTunes API and put ours next to them at 60px. That's what finally made the direction obvious.



\- Store screenshots: six rounds. I'd point it at games that sell well, it would download their store pages, work out the layout, and mock ours up. I killed rounds two and three for looking AI-made: glowing light, gold gradient text, thin gold borders. Those exact words are now in its notes under "never do this".



\- Bug audits: four times I said "go find everything that's broken". It split the game into areas, ran one agent per area in its own git worktree, each one writing a repro script before touching anything, then merged the fixes one by one with the full test suite between each merge. Well over a hundred fixes came out of those.



What actually mattered:



\- The notes file. Every decision, every "tried this, broke because of that", with a date. It got so big we recently split it into a dozen files. Without it, every new session re-proposes things I rejected weeks ago.



\- A headless test suite (about 20k checks) plus a fast subset for small changes. Full run only for big bundles. Waiting a minute per typo fix kills the pace.



\- Two bots. One plays the game for balance numbers. The other plays the tutorial like a person would, tapping whatever the hint points at. The tutorial bot found things like "the hint says tap this spell, the spell is out of range".



\- A script that screenshots every screen in the game. "Done, all tests pass" has meant "a button is off the edge of the screen" more times than I can count. Apple rejected us twice for exactly that before I made the screenshot check mandatory.



\- Seeded everything. Same seed, same floor. Hand it a seed and it reproduces the bug itself.



\- It cannot judge its own art or sound. Never could. I was the eyes and ears for every single asset.



What went badly:



\- I tried a "studio" setup: a director agent writing work orders, departments (gameplay, level design, art, audio, balance), a reviewer at the end. It was slow. Now I dispatch directly and only keep the extra review for rule changes.



\- Launching twenty agents at once hit the usage limit and killed all of them mid-task.



\- A Korean roguelike community tore the game apart, partly because a promo comic was AI-drawn and I hadn't said so. AI use is now the first thing in every post, including this one.



\- It once ran a scene script in an infinite loop and filled my disk with a 1.8GB log in three minutes.



The game: turn-based, permadeath, built out of Korean folktales. The grim reaper calls your name every turn he can see you. A serpent turns into a dragon if you take too long to kill it. Eight gods with taboos, 14 species, 12 classes.



Free, offline, no account. One purchase unlocks extra species and classes, one optional ad to revive. Code written with Claude Code, sprites script-generated, music CC BY, SFX synthesized in Python. The design calls and the playtesting are mine.



App Store: [https://apps.apple.com/app/id6814757012](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6814757012)

Google Play: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sungkisoft.seolhwadungeon&referrer=utm\_source%3Dreddit%26utm\_medium%3Dpost%26utm\_campaign%3Daigamedev](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sungkisoft.seolhwadungeon&referrer=utm_source%3Dreddit%26utm_medium%3Dpost%26utm_campaign%3Daigamedev)



Happy to answer anything about the workflow. Still patching every other day.
